The commentary of Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) on the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder (1). But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition (2).﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) differed about the meaning of the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿Sad﴾. Some of them said: it is from al-musada (confronting, comparing), from "sadaytu fulanan" (I confronted so-and-so), and it is an imperative from that. Their meaning is: "Sad your deeds against the Qur'an," i.e., "present them to it" (aridh bihi). Whoever holds this interpretation reads it with a kasra on the dal, because it is an imperative. This was also narrated from al-Hasan.

Mention of the narration to that effect:

- Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, on the authority of Qatadah, who said: al-Hasan said, regarding ﴿Sad﴾: "Confront the Qur'an" (haditha al-Qur'an).

- I was told on the authority of Ali ibn Asim, on the authority of Amr ibn Ubayd, on the authority of al-Hasan, regarding His words ﴿Sad﴾, he said: "Present the Qur'an with your deeds."

- I was told on the authority of Abd al-Wahhab, on the authority of Sa'id, on the authority of Qatadah, on the authority of al-Hasan, regarding His words ﴿Sad, by the Qur'an﴾, he said: "Present the Qur'an." Abd al-Wahhab said: He means, "Present it against your deeds, and see where your deeds stand in relation to the Qur'an."

- Ahmad ibn Yusuf told me, saying: al-Qasim told us, saying: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Harun, on the authority of Isma'il, on the authority of al-Hasan, that he used to read ﴿Sad, by the Qur'an﴾ with a kasra on the dal, and he would make it from al-musada, saying: "Present the Qur'an."

Others said: it is a letter of the alphabet (huruf hija').

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn al-Husayn told me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal told us, saying: Asbat told us, on the authority of al-Suddi: As for ﴿Sad﴾, it is among the letters (of the alphabet).

Others said: it is an oath which Allah swore by.

Mention of those who said that:

- Ali told me, saying: Abu Salih told us, saying: Mu'awiyah told me, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿Sad﴾, he said: "It is an oath that Allah swore, and it is one of the names of Allah."

Others said: it is one of the names of the Qur'an, by which Allah swore.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, on the authority of Qatadah, regarding ﴿Sad﴾, he said: "It is one of the names of the Qur'an, by which Allah swore."

Others said: its meaning is "Allah has spoken truly" (sadaqa Allah).

Mention of those who said that:

- I was told on the authority of al-Musayyab ibn Sharik, on the authority of Abu Ruq, on the authority of al-Dahhak, regarding His words ﴿Sad﴾, he said: "Allah has spoken truly."

The readers differed in their recitation of this. The common readers of the major cities (qurra' al-amsar) read it with a sukun on the dal, except for Abd Allah ibn Abi Ishaq and Isa ibn Umar. As for Abd Allah ibn Abi Ishaq, he used to give it a kasra because of the meeting of two sakin letters (ijtima' al-sakinayn), and he treated it as a particle of the same kind as the Arabs' saying: "tarakahu hath bath" and "khaz baz" (expressions meaning "he left him in disorder"), the two of which are pronounced with a kasra when the final letter is an alif, and with a fath when it is otherwise, saying "hayth bayth," and "la-ajʿalannaka fi hays bays," meaning when one is constrained. As for Isa ibn Umar, he used to match all the forms in which the letter before the last was an alif, and those in which the letter before the last was a ya' or a waw, by giving all of them a fath and making them accusative, saying: "Sa, Qa, Na, Ya-Sin," treating them like particles, as in their saying "layta" (would that), "ayna" (where), and similar.

The correct reading in our view is the sukun in all of these, because the reading that the common readers of the cities have transmitted is widely established among them, and because these are letters of the alphabet naming what they name. They are inflected in the manner of nouns, particles and sounds, and they are treated according to that pattern. Thus their interpretation, since they are of this kind, is the interpretation of their counterparts that were explained earlier.

Some of the grammarians of Arabic said: the meaning of ﴿Sad﴾ is like your saying "wajab wallah" (it is binding, by Allah), "nazal wallah" (it has descended, by Allah), and "haqq wallah" (it is true, by Allah), and it is the answer to His words ﴿and the Qur'an﴾, just as you say "haqqan wallah" (truly, by Allah) and "nazal wallah."

* *

As for His words ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾:

This is an oath which Allah, blessed and exalted, swore by this Qur'an, saying: ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾.

The interpreters differed about the meaning of His words ﴿full of reminder (dhi al-dhikr)﴾. Some of them said: it means "full of honour" (dhi al-sharaf).

Mention of those who said that:

- Nasr ibn Ali told us, saying: Abu Ahmad told us, on the authority of Qays, on the authority of Abu Husayn, on the authority of Sa'id, regarding ﴿Sad, by the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, he said: "full of honour."

- Nasr ibn Ali and Ibn Bashshar told us, both saying: Abu Ahmad told us, on the authority of Mis'ar, on the authority of Abu Husayn, regarding ﴿full of reminder﴾: "full of honour."

- He said: Abu Ahmad told us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Isma'il, on the authority of Abu Salih or someone else, regarding ﴿full of reminder﴾: "full of honour."

- Muhammad ibn al-Husayn told us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal told us, saying: Asbat told us, on the authority of al-Suddi, regarding ﴿by the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, he said: "full of honour."

- Abu Kurayb told us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Hisham told us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Yahya ibn Umarah, on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿Sad, by the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾: "full of honour."

Others said: rather, its meaning is "full of admonition," in which Allah reminded you.

Mention of those who said that:

- I was told on the authority of al-Musayyab ibn Sharik, on the authority of Abu Ruq, on the authority of al-Dahhak, regarding ﴿full of reminder﴾, he said: "In it is your reminder." He said: a parallel to it is His words ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾.

- Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, on the authority of Qatadah, regarding ﴿full of reminder﴾: "that is, what is mentioned in it."

The most correct of the two views, in our opinion, is the view of the one who said: its meaning is "full of admonition to you," because Allah followed it with His words ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾. Thus it was known from this that He was informing about the Qur'an that He sent it down as a reminder to His servants, by which He reminds them, and that the disbelievers are in arrogance and opposition against believing in it.

They differed about what the oath's object is. Some of them said: the oath falls upon His words ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾.

Mention of those who said that:

- Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, on the authority of Qatadah: ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance﴾, he said: "Here is where the oath falls."

Some of the grammarians of Arabic said: "bal" (but/rather) is evidence of their denial, so "bal" was made to suffice as the answer to the oath, as if it were said: "Sad, the matter is not as you say; rather, you are in arrogance and opposition." Some grammarians of Kufa said: "They claim that the place of the oath is in His words ﴿There is none but has denied the messengers﴾." Another Kufan grammarian said: "Some people have claimed that the answer to ﴿and the Qur'an﴾ is His words ﴿Indeed, that is true: the disputing of the people of the Fire﴾." He said: That is a statement that has been delayed a great deal from His words ﴿and the Qur'an﴾, and other accounts have intervened between them, so we do not find this sound in Arabic, and Allah knows best.

He said: It is said that His words ﴿and the Qur'an﴾ are an oath interrupted by speech placed before the position of its answer, so the answer belongs to both the interruption and the oath. So it is as if He intended: "By the Qur'an, full of reminder, indeed We destroyed [many generations before them]," and when His words ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance﴾ intervened, "kam" became the answer to both the "arrogance" and the oath. He said: Similarly His words ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾, where His words ﴿and by the soul and Him who proportioned it and inspired it﴾ intervened before the answer, so "qad aflaha" (he has succeeded) follows His words "fa-alhamaha" (and inspired it), and it suffices as the answer to the oath. It is as if He said: "By the sun and its brightness, he has indeed succeeded."

The correct view on this matter, in my judgment, is the view stated by Qatadah: since "bal" indicates denial and occupies the position of the answer, it suffices in place of the answer once the meaning is known. Thus the meaning of the sentence, given that this is the case, is: ﴿Sad, by the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, [it is not so], as these disbelievers say; rather, they are in arrogance and opposition.

* *

As for His words ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾:

He, may His mention be exalted, says: Rather, those among the polytheists of Quraysh who disbelieve in Allah are in partisanship and enmity, and in separation from Muhammad and hostility toward him. And there is nothing wrong with them that they should not be people of knowledge that he is neither a sorcerer nor a liar.

The interpreters have spoken in accordance with what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Amr told me, saying: Abu Asim told us, saying: Isa told us; and al-Harith told me, saying: al-Hasan told us, saying: Warqa' told us, all of them on the authority of Ibn Abi Najih, on the authority of Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿in arrogance and opposition﴾, he said: "Resisting one another (mu'azzin)."

- Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, on the authority of Qatadah, regarding ﴿in arrogance and opposition﴾: "that is, in zeal (hamiyya) and separation (firaq)."

- Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾: "They oppose the command of Allah, His messengers and His Book, and they contend against them; that is arrogance and opposition." I said to him: "Opposition (shiqaq) means dispute (khilaf)?" He said: "Yes."

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: How many did We destroy before these polytheists of Quraysh, who denied Our Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) in what he brought them from Us of the truth. ﴿Generations﴾ means: nations who were before them; they followed their path in denying their messengers in what the messengers brought them from God. ﴿And they cried out﴾ means: they cried out to their Lord, shouted, and sought relief by repenting to Him, when God's punishment descended upon them and they witnessed His torment, fleeing from His retribution and escaping from His painful punishment. ﴿But there was no time for escape﴾ means: that was not a time for fleeing or escaping the punishment through repentance, for the word of punishment had already been fulfilled against them; they repented when repentance would not benefit them, and they asked for reprieve at a time when reprieve was not granted.

* *

As for His words ﴿manāṣ﴾ (escape):

It is a form of mafʿal from al-nawṣ. In the language of the Arabs, al-nawṣ means to draw back, and al-manāṣ means a place of escape. Hence the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

Is it from remembering Salmā, when she moved far from you ... so that you draw back from her a step and advance?

[The line is from Imru' al-Qays, in Mukhtar al-Shi'r al-Jahili, with the commentary of Mustafa al-Saqqa, Halabi edition, 127. He said: "na'at-ka": she went far from you. "Tanūṣ": she draws back; "faqṣuru 'anhā": one says "aqṣara 'anhu khaṭwahu" when he restrains it from him. "Watabūṣ": she advances. He means: is it because she has moved far from you, and you remember her and yearn for her, that you should draw back from her, and shorten your speech toward her, or advance toward her, eager in her pursuit? The line is among the evidences of al-Farrā' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (276), where he said, explaining His words "wa-lāta ḥīna manāṣ": he means: it is not a time of flight. Al-nawṣ in the speech of the Arabs is drawing back, and al-bawṣ is advancing. Imru' al-Qays said: "Amin dhikri..." the line. So manāṣ is a mafʿal, like maqām. Some Arabs add "lāt" and put it in the genitive. They recited to me: "Lāta sā'ati mandam." End.]

He says: or advance. It is said from this: nāṣanī fulān, meaning he went away from you; bāṣanī, meaning he outstripped you; and nāḍa fī al-bilād, meaning he went off into the lands, with a ḍād. Al-Farrā' mentioned that al-ʿUqaylī recited to him:

When Isḥāq lives and his sheikh, I do not care
about a loss, and departing from me is not difficult.

[The author says: al-Farrā' mentioned that al-ʿUqaylī recited the two lines to him. It is understood from this that al-Farrā' transmitted the two lines in Ma'ani al-Qur'an while explaining His words "wa-lāta ḥīna manāṣ," so perhaps they are in a copy other than the one in our hands. The author of Lisan al-ʿArab cited the second line under (khaḍḍa) and said before it: al-khiḍāḍ is a small piece of jewelry, and he recited al-Qannānī: "Wa-law ashrafat..." I say: perhaps the words al-ʿUqaylī and al-Qannānī are corrupted, one from the other. The place of evidence in the first line is in his word "manāḍ," meaning departure into the land; it is a mimi verbal noun. It is close in meaning to manāṣ with the unpointed ṣād, meaning a place of escape. In Lisan (nawḍ): nāḍa fulān yanūḍu nawḍan fī al-bilād, like nāṣa 'adl. End.]

And if she had looked out from the edge of the curtain, adorned,
I would have said: a gazelle, upon which there is no jewelry.

Khuḍāḍ: jewelry.

Those of the exegetical tradition said similarly to what we have said.

He said: It is not a time for leaping nor for flight, the people being restrained.

⁕ Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, saying: Ḥakkām related to us, from ʿAnbasa, from Abū Isḥāq al-Hamdānī, from al-Tamīmī, who said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbās about God's words ﴿but there was no time for escape﴾. He said: It is not a time of leaping nor of flight.

⁕ Muḥammad ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words ﴿but there was no time for escape﴾. He said: It is not a time of leaping nor of flight.

⁕ ʿAlī related to me, saying: ʿAbd Allāh related to us, saying: Muʿāwiya related to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words ﴿but there was no time for escape﴾: he says: it is not a time of rescue.

⁕ Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, saying: ʿĪsā related to us, and al-Ḥārith related to me, saying: al-Ḥasan related to us, saying: Warqā' related to us, all from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding God's words ﴿but there was no time for escape﴾: He said: This is not a time of flight.

⁕ Bishr related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatāda, regarding ﴿and they cried out, but there was no time for escape﴾: He said: The people called out at a time that was not a time for calling, and they wished to repent when they witnessed God's punishment, but that was not accepted from them.

⁕ Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn related to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn al-Mufaḍḍal related to us, saying: Asbāṭ related to us, from al-Suddī, regarding His words ﴿but there was no time for escape﴾: He said: When the punishment descended upon them, they were unable to return to repentance, nor to flee from the punishment.

⁕ I was told from al-Ḥusayn, who said: I heard Abū Muʿādh say: ʿUbayd related to us, saying: I heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say, regarding His words ﴿and they cried out, but there was no time for escape﴾: He says: It is not a time of flight.

⁕ Yūnus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿but there was no time for escape﴾: "There was no time of escape for them to escape from." The word "ḥīn" in His words ﴿but there was no time for escape﴾ is in the accusative, as a likening of lāt to laysa, and a subject-noun (ism al-fāʿil) was implied within it.

Some of the grammarians of Basra related the nominative with lāt in ḥīn, claiming that some of them read "wa-lāta ḥīnu manāṣin," making it like the words of laysa, as if he said: laysa, and the ḥīn was implied. He said: And in poetry:

They sought our reconciliation, but it was no longer time,
So we answered that there was no time for survival.

[This line belongs to Abū Zubayd al-Mundhir ibn Ḥarmala al-Ṭāʾī the Christian, who lived to see Islam. ʿUthmān (raḍiya Allāh ʿanhu) used to draw him near and bring him close to his assembly (Farā'id al-Qalā'id, in the abridgement of Sharḥ al-Shawāhid, by al-ʿAynī). He said: The evidence is in his words "wa-lāta awān," where the noun awān is the predicate of lāt, like ḥīn: meaning awān is not the time of reconciliation. The genitive is omitted, then awān is built, as qabl and baʿd are built when the genitive is omitted, but it is built on kasra, likening it to nazāl in form, then nunated for necessity. And "an" is explanatory. It is not for negation, and its subject is omitted. And "ḥīna baqā'" is its predicate: meaning the time is not the time of the survival of reconciliation. End. Al-Farrā' said after his statement that we quoted under the previous evidence: Someone recited to me: "They sought our reconciliation..." so he put awān in the genitive. End. I say: he did not say that it was built on kasra.]

So he put awān in the genitive and implied ḥīn with awān, because lāt is only used with ḥīn. He said: lāt is used only with ḥīn. Some grammarians of Kufa said: Some Arabs add lāt and put a noun in the genitive after it. He mentioned that he recited:

Lāt sāʿata mandam [a fragment of a line; in full, as in Farā'id al-Qalā'id by al-ʿAynī (p. 105, separate from al-Khizāna of al-Baghdādī):
They regretted, and it was not the hour for regret ... and rebellion is a pasture whose seeker is harmed.]

In al-ʿAynī's transmission, the reading is with the accusative of sāʿa, not the genitive. He said in his commentary that its speaker was Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā ibn Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh al-Taymī, and it was said Muhalhil ibn Mālik al-Kinānī. Al-Farrā' said, after reciting the line (276) and the discussion: that it is in the sense of laysa to be governed by it. End. I say: In al-Khizāna al-Adab of al-Baghdādī (2: 144–147) there is much debate among the grammarians about the i'rāb of "sāʿa" in the line; the accusative is the well-known transmission, and al-Farrā' agreed with it at the end of his speech. As for the genitive, he relates it from one who recited this fragment, whose first hemistich he said he does not remember; al-Farrā' did not accept the genitive with lāt, and decided that the proper construction is the accusative with it, because it means laysa, and he cited the next evidence, confirming his statement on its governing of the accusative.

As for the transmission of the line, we have mentioned its version from Ibn ʿAqīl and other commentators on the Alfiyya, attributed to a man of Ṭayyiʾ. In al-Khizāna (2: 147), Ibn al-Sikkīt transmitted it in Kitāb al-Aḍdād, and it is: "Wa-lataʿrifanna khalā'iqan mashmūlatan / wa-latandamanna wa-lāta sāʿata mandami." Ibn al-Aʿrābī said, explaining "mashmūlatan": it is said akhlāq mashmūla, meaning ill-omened, and bad character. He said: It is also said: a man of mashmūl dispositions, meaning of noble character. End.

with the genitive of "sāʿa." He said: The construction is that it governs the accusative, because it means laysa. He mentioned that he recited:

Tadhakkara ḥubba Laylā lāta ḥīnan / wa-aḍḥā al-shaybu qad qaṭaʿa al-qarīnā

[The line is among the evidences of al-Farrā' (folio 276) that lāt governs the accusative of what follows it. In Ma'ani al-Qur'an, explaining the aspect of governing with lāt, he said: The statement is that it governs the accusative, in the sense of laysa. Al-Mufaḍḍal recited to me: "Tadhakkara ḥubb..." the line. Then he said after it: This is accusative. Then he recited another evidence for the genitive with it, which is the poet's words: "They sought our reconciliation, but it was no longer time..." the line. End.]

He said: One of them recited to me:

They sought our reconciliation, and lāt awānin / so we answered that there was no time for survival.

[The line was discussed shortly before; refer to its place.]

with the genitive of "awānin." He said: lāt is used with all times.

They differed about the manner of pausing according to the reading "lāta ḥīna." Some grammarians of Arabic said: pause on it as "lāt" with a tā', then begin "ḥīna manāṣ." They said: it is only "lā" in the sense of "mā," and in negation it was joined with a tā', just as thumma was joined with it and it became thumma, and as rubba was joined and it became rubbat.

Others said: rather, it is a hā' added to lā, so the pause on it is "lāh," because it is a hā' added for pausing, just as it was added in their saying:

Al-ʿāṭifūnah ḥīna mā min ʿāṭif / wa-al-muṭʿimūnah ḥīna ayna al-muṭʿamu

[This evidence was also recited by the author of al-Khizāna (2: 147), who quoted many grammarians' views on its explanation. Among the best explanations is Ibn Jinnī's saying, which the author of al-Khizāna quoted from Ibn Jinnī's Sirr Ṣinā'at al-I'rāb. He said: Ibn al-Sīrāfī preceded him in the commentary on the strange evidences, and Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī in al-Masā'il al-Manthūra. It is that the tā' in "al-ʿāṭifūnah" was originally the hā' of pausing, attached to "al-ʿāṭifūn"; the poet was forced to move it, so he changed it to tā' and made it fatḥa. Ibn Jinnī said: he wanted to keep it in its original state as it is in pausing. That is, one says in pausing: "hā'ulā' muslimūnah" and "ḍāribūnah," so the hā' is attached to show the movement of the nūn. So the expression became "al-ʿāṭifūnah." Then he likened the hā' of pausing to the hā' of feminine marking; when he needed the movement of the hā' to complete the meter, he turned it into a tā', just as you say in pausing "hādhā Ṭalḥah," and when connected it becomes "hādhihi Ṭalḥatunā." On this he said "al-ʿāṭifūnah." He said: What supports the soundness of this is the saying of the rajaz poet: "Min baʿdi mā wa-baʿdi mā wa-baʿdi mit / ṣārat nufūs al-qawmi ʿinda al-ghalṣamit." He meant "wa-baʿda mā," so he changed the alif in the estimate, making it "baʿdimah," then changed the hā' into a tā' to agree with the rest of the rhymes that follow. The likeness of the estimated hā' in "wa-baʿdimah" to the hā' of feminine marking in "Ṭalḥah" and "Ḥamzah" encouraged him to do so... End. Ibn Mālik mentioned in al-Tashīl that the tā' is the remnant of lāt, so lā was dropped and the tā' remained, and sometimes with estimation one dispenses with lā by the tā'... End. The line is from a qaṣīda by Abū Wajza al-Saʿdī, praising the family of al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām, but it is composed of the two halves of two lines; the second half of it is: "wa-al-musbighūna yadan idhā mā anʿamū."]

So when it is connected, it becomes tā'. Some said: the pause is on "lā," and the beginning after it is "taḥīn," claiming that the rule of the tā' is that it is at the beginning of "ḥīn," "awān," and "al-ān," and they cite for this saying the verse of a poet:

Tawallā qabla yawmi sabyin Jumānā / wa-ṣalīnā kamā zaʿamti Talānā

[The line belongs to ʿAmr ibn Aḥmar al-Bāhilī, as in footnote 1 of the first part of Sirr Ṣinā'at al-I'rāb, Halabi edition, 185; its version in the original is: "Nuwallī qabla nā'ī dār Jumānā / wa-ṣalīhi kamā zaʿamti Talānā." Ibn al-Anbārī in al-Insāf fī Masā'il al-Khilāf (Leiden edition, 1913, p. 51) has: "Nuwallī qabla yawmi nā'ī Jumānā / wa-ṣalīnā kamā zaʿamti Talānā." Nuwallī: from al-nawāl, originally giving; what is meant here is what the lover is provided with from the beloved. Jumānā: a diminutive of Jumāna, a woman's name, and the alif is for elongation. The evidence is in "Talānā," where he added a tā' before al-ān, as a tā' is added before ḥīn.]

He claims there is no "lā" here to which a hā' or tā' is attached, and says that His words ﴿lāta ḥīn﴾ are only "laysa ḥīn," and that lāt is not found in any speech.

The correct view on this matter, in our opinion, is that "lā" is a particle of negation, as it is; and when it is connected, it becomes a tā' in connection, as the Arabs did with particles. They did not use this with the lengthened "lā" except for times, and not otherwise. There is no basis for the reason given by the one who said he did not find lāt in any Arab speech, so His words ﴿wa-lāta ḥīn﴾ may be interpreted in that way, since they use the word in one place and then use it in another place differently. This is no more remote in analogy from soundness than their saying "ra'aytu" with the hamza, and then they say "fa-anā arāh" without the hamza, following their usage; and similar letters that come in one form in one place and differently in another, following the usage of the Arabs among themselves. As for what he cited of the poet's words, "Wa-ka-mā zaʿamti Talānā," it is an error in the interpretation of the word: the poet meant by his words "wa-ṣalīnā kamā zaʿamti Talānā": "and we connected as you claim now," dropping the hamza from "anta," so the tā' of "zaʿamti" met the nūn of "anta," which was quiescent, so it fell out of pronunciation, and the tā' of "anta" remained; then the hamza of "al-ān" was dropped, so the word in pronunciation became like "Talān." The second tā' is in reality separate from "al-ān," because it is the tā' of "anta." As for his claim that he saw in the codex called the Imam the tā' joined to ḥīn, what the copies of the Muslims in their regions brought is the proof against the people of Islam, and the tā' in all of them is separated from ḥīn. Therefore we have chosen that the pause be on the hā' in His words ﴿wa-lāta ḥīn﴾.

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 38, verses 4–5:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves, and the disbelievers say, "This is a sorcerer, a liar." (4) "Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing."﴾ (5)

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: These polytheists of Quraysh wondered that a warner had come to them, one who warns them of God's punishment for their disbelief in Him, from among themselves, and that no angel had come down from heaven with this message. ﴿And the disbelievers said, "This is a sorcerer, a liar."﴾ That is: those who deny God's oneness said, "This one," meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), "is a sorcerer, a liar."

The people of ta'wil (interpretation) have said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said this:

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿And they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿and the disbelievers said, "This is a sorcerer, a liar."﴾

* Muhammad related to us, saying: Ahmad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿a sorcerer, a liar﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

* * *

As for His words ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾

That is: those disbelievers who said, "Muhammad is a sorcerer, a liar," said: Has Muhammad made all the objects of worship into one, one that hears all our supplications and knows the worship of each worshipper among us? ﴿Indeed, this is a strange thing﴾: that is, indeed this is a wondrous thing.

As follows:

* Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing.﴾ He said: The polytheists were astonished that they were called to worship God alone, and they said: One god hears all our needs together! We have not heard of this in the latter religion.

The reason for the saying of these polytheists, which God reported that they said, was as follows: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "I ask you to respond to me with one word, by which the Arabs will submit to you and by which the non-Arabs will pay you the kharaj (land tax)." They said: "And what is it?" He said: "You say: There is no god but God." At that they said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾, in astonishment at that.

Those who said this:

* Abu Kurayb and Ibn Wakī' related to us, both saying: Abu Usama related to us, saying: al-A'mash related to us, saying: Abbad related to us, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: When Abu Talib fell ill, a group of Quraysh entered upon him, among them Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, and they said: "Your nephew insults our gods, and does this and that, and says this and that. So if you sent for him and forbade him?" So he sent for him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) came and entered the house, and between them and Abu Talib was the space of one man's seat. He said: Abu Jahl feared that if he sat beside Abu Talib, he would be more tender toward him, so he leapt up and sat in that seat, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) found no seat near his uncle, so he sat by the door. Abu Talib said to him: "O my nephew, what is it with your people complaining about you? They claim you insult their gods, and say this and that." He said: They pressed their words upon him, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) spoke, saying: "O uncle, I want them to adopt one word which they would say, by which the Arabs would submit to them and by which the non-Arabs would pay them the jizya (poll tax)." They were startled by his word and his statement. The people said: "One word? Yes, by your father, ten!" They said: "And what is it?" Abu Talib said: "And what word is it, O my nephew?" He said: "There is no god but God." He said: They stood up alarmed, shaking out their garments, saying: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing.﴾ He said: And from this place to His words ﴿not yet have they tasted My punishment﴾ was revealed. The wording is that of Abu Kurayb.

* Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Hisham related to us, from Sufyan, from Yahya ibn Umara, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Abu Talib fell ill, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to visit him, while they were sitting around him, and at his head there was an empty place. Abu Jahl stood up and sat in it. Abu Talib said: "O my nephew, what is it with your people complaining about you?" He said: "O uncle, I want them to adopt one word, by which the Arabs would submit to them and by which the non-Arabs would pay them the jizya." He said: "What is it?" He said: "There is no god but God." They stood up saying: ﴿We have not heard of this in the latter religion. This is nothing but a fabrication.﴾ And the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, full of honour, ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾, up to His words ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾.

* Ibn Wakī' related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id related to us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Yahya ibn Umara, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Abu Talib fell ill, then he mentioned something similar, except that he did not say "full of honour," and he said: up to His words ﴿Indeed, this is a strange thing.﴾

* Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from al-A'mash, from Yahya ibn Umara, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Abu Talib fell ill. He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) came to visit him, and at his head was the seat of a man. Abu Jahl stood up and sat in it. They complained about the Prophet (ﷺ) to Abu Talib, and said: "He attacks our gods." He said: "O my nephew, what do you want with this?" He said: "O uncle, I want them to adopt one word, by which the Arabs would submit to them and by which the non-Arabs would pay them the jizya." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "There is no god but God." Then they said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing.﴾

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 38, verses 6–7:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth, saying: "Walk on, and be steadfast in [the worship of] your gods. Indeed, this is a thing that is intended. We have not heard of this in the latter religion. This is not but a fabrication."﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: The nobles from among these disbelievers of Quraysh went forth, those who were saying: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾, [saying] to one another: walk on and be steadfast in your religion and in the worship of your gods. Those who said this:

* Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, that some people of Quraysh gathered, among them Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, al-ʿAs ibn Wa’il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth, along with a group of the elders of Quraysh. Some of them said to others: "Let us go to Abu Talib, and speak to him about this, so that he may deal justly with us regarding him, and command him to desist from reviling our gods, and we will leave him and his god whom he worships, for we fear that this old man may die, and something will happen between us, and the Arabs will reproach us, saying: 'They left him until his uncle died, then they attacked him.'" He said: they sent a man from among them called al-Mutallib, who asked permission for them to enter upon Abu Talib. He said: "These are the elders of your people and their chiefs, asking permission to see you." He said: "Let them in." When they entered upon him, they said: "O Abu Talib, you are our senior and our leader; deal justly with us concerning your nephew, so command him to desist from reviling our gods, and we will leave him and his god." He said: then Abu Talib sent for him. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon him, he said: "O nephew, these are the elders of your people and their chiefs, and they have asked you for fairness: that you desist from reviling their gods, and they will leave you and your god." He said: [the Prophet] said: "O uncle, shall I not call them to what is better for them than that?" He said: "And to what will you call them?" He said: "I call them to a word by which the Arabs will submit to them and by which they will rule over the non-Arabs." He said: Abu Jahl said from among the people: "What is it, by your father? We will certainly give it to you, and ten times its like." He said: "You say: There is no god but Allah." He said: they recoiled and said: "Ask us for something other than this." He said: "Even if you brought me the sun to place in my hand, I would not ask you for anything other than it." He said: they became angry, stood up from his presence in wrath, and said: "By Allah, we will revile you and whoever commands you with this." So ﴿And the chiefs among them went forth, saying: "Walk on, and be steadfast in [the worship of] your gods. Indeed, this is a thing that is intended"﴾ ... to His saying ﴿This is not but a fabrication﴾. He turned to his uncle, and his uncle said to him: "O nephew, you have not been harsh with them." Then he turned to his uncle and called him, and said: "Say one word by which I will testify for you on the Day of Resurrection: say, 'There is no god but Allah.'" He said: "Were it not that the Arabs would reproach you, saying, 'He panicked at death,' I would have given it to you; but [I will remain] upon the religion of the elders." He said: then this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 38, verses 8–9:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him from among us?  Nay, but they are in doubt about My Reminder. Nay, but they have not yet tasted My punishment.  Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Mighty, the Bestower?﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says, relating the speech of these polytheists from Quraysh: "Has the Reminder been sent down to Muhammad from among us, so that he was singled out for it, when he is not nobler than us in lineage?"

* *

As for His saying ﴿Nay, but they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: It is not that these polytheists lack knowledge that Muhammad is truthful, but they are in doubt about Our revelation to him, and about this Qur'an which We sent down to him, that it is from Us. ﴿Nay, but they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾. He says: Rather, Our wrath has not yet descended upon them, so that they taste the consequence of their denial of Muhammad and their doubt about Our sending down this Qur'an to him. Had they tasted the punishment for that, they would have known and become certain of the reality of what they were denying, at a time when their knowledge would no longer benefit them.

﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Mighty, the Bestower?﴾ He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Or do these polytheists who deny the revelation of God to Muhammad possess the treasuries of your Lord's mercy, meaning the keys to your Lord's mercy, O Muhammad, the Mighty in His dominion, the Bestower upon whomever He wills of His creation, whatever He wills of kingdom, authority and prophethood? So that they could prevent you, O Muhammad, from the honour with which God has favoured you and the messengership with which He has preferred you.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 38, verses 10–11:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they possess the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them? Then let them ascend by the means.﴾ ﴿A host, defeated there, from among the factions.﴾

He, exalted is His mention, says: Or do these polytheists, who are in arrogance and opposition, possess ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾? For no one who is within My dominion and authority can contend against Me or oppose Me.

* *

As for His saying ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾:

He says: If they possess the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, then let them ascend through the gates and paths of the sky, for whoever has dominion over something should not find it impossible to oversee it and to attend to it.

The people of interpretation differed concerning the meaning of "the means" (al-asbab) mentioned by God in this place. Some of them said: it refers to the gates of the sky.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾: he said: the paths of the sky and its gates.

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾: he said: into the gates of the sky.

Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿by the means﴾: he said: the means of the heavens.

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾: he said: the paths of the heavens.

It has been related to me from al-Muharibi, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding ﴿Or do they possess the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: he said: meaning, if ﴿they possess the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, then let them ascend by the means﴾; he said: let them ascend to the seventh heaven.

Ali related to me, saying: Abdullah related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾: he said: into the sky.

It is mentioned from al-Rabi ibn Anas concerning this what has been related to me from al-Musayyib ibn Shurayk, from Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from al-Rabi ibn Anas, who said: "The asbab are finer than hair, harder than iron, and they are everywhere, except that they are not seen."

The original meaning of sabab (means) among the Arabs is: everything by which one makes a connection to reach a desired object, whether a rope or a means, a kinship or relationship, a road or a path, or other such things.

* *

As for His saying ﴿A host, defeated there, from among the factions﴾:

He, exalted is His mention, says: they are ﴿a host﴾, meaning those who are in arrogance and opposition, ﴿there﴾, meaning: at Badr, ﴿defeated﴾.

* *

As for His saying ﴿there﴾:

It is connected to "defeated." His saying ﴿from among the factions﴾ means: from among the factions of Iblis and his followers who passed before them, whom God destroyed for their sins. The "min" in ﴿min al-ahzab﴾ is connected to the word "host," and the meaning of the statement is: they are a host from among the factions, defeated there. And the "ma" in ﴿jundun ma hunalika﴾ is an extra particle (silah).

The people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿A host, defeated there, from among the factions﴾: he said: Quraysh are among the factions; he said: the past generations.

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿A host, defeated there, from among the factions﴾: he said: God promised him, while he was in Makkah on that day, that He would defeat a host of the polytheists, and its fulfillment came on the day of Badr.

Some of the Arabic grammarians interpreted ﴿jundun ma hunalika﴾ as: defeated, unable to ascend into the sky.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 38, verses 10–11:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they possess the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them? Then let them ascend by the means.﴾ ﴿A host, defeated there, from among the factions.﴾

He, exalted is His mention, says: Or do these polytheists, who are in arrogance and opposition, possess ﴿the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾? For no one who is within My dominion and authority can contend against Me or oppose Me.

* *

As for His saying ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾:

He says: If they possess the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, then let them ascend through the gates and paths of the sky, for whoever has dominion over something should not find it impossible to oversee it and to attend to it.

The people of interpretation differed concerning the meaning of "the means" (al-asbab) mentioned by God in this place. Some of them said: it refers to the gates of the sky.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾: he said: the paths of the sky and its gates.

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾: he said: into the gates of the sky.

Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿by the means﴾: he said: the means of the heavens.

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾: he said: the paths of the heavens.

It has been related to me from al-Muharibi, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding ﴿Or do they possess the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: he said: meaning, if ﴿they possess the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, then let them ascend by the means﴾; he said: let them ascend to the seventh heaven.

Ali related to me, saying: Abdullah related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾: he said: into the sky.

It is mentioned from al-Rabi ibn Anas concerning this what has been related to me from al-Musayyib ibn Shurayk, from Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from al-Rabi ibn Anas, who said: "The asbab are finer than hair, harder than iron, and they are everywhere, except that they are not seen."

The original meaning of sabab (means) among the Arabs is: everything by which one makes a connection to reach a desired object, whether a rope or a means, a kinship or relationship, a road or a path, or other such things.

* *

As for His saying ﴿A host, defeated there, from among the factions﴾:

He, exalted is His mention, says: they are ﴿a host﴾, meaning those who are in arrogance and opposition, ﴿there﴾, meaning: at Badr, ﴿defeated﴾.

* *

As for His saying ﴿there﴾:

It is connected to "defeated." His saying ﴿from among the factions﴾ means: from among the factions of Iblis and his followers who passed before them, whom God destroyed for their sins. The "min" in ﴿min al-ahzab﴾ is connected to the word "host," and the meaning of the statement is: they are a host from among the factions, defeated there. And the "ma" in ﴿jundun ma hunalika﴾ is an extra particle (silah).

The people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿A host, defeated there, from among the factions﴾: he said: Quraysh are among the factions; he said: the past generations.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 38, verse 12–14:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Before them the people of Noah, and ʿĀd, and Pharaoh, the one of the pegs, denied (their messengers)﴾ [12] ﴿and Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the Thicket. Those are the factions﴾ [13] ﴿Each one of them denied the messengers, so My punishment was justly due﴾ [14].

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Before these polytheists of Quraysh, who say, "Does he make the gods into one god?", there denied their messengers the people of Noah, ʿĀd, and Pharaoh, the one of the pegs.

The scholars differed concerning the reason for which Pharaoh was called "the one of the pegs." Some of them said: He was called that because he had playgrounds made of pegs, on which people would play for him.

Those who said this:

⁕ I was told by ʿAlī ibn al-Haytham, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Jaʿfar, from his father, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding ﴿and Pharaoh, the one of the pegs﴾, that he said: "They were playgrounds under which he would be played for."

⁕ Bishr told us, saying: Yazīd told us, saying: Saʿīd told us, from Qatādah, regarding his saying ﴿and Pharaoh, the one of the pegs﴾, that he said: "He had pegs and ropes, and playgrounds on which people would play for him."

Others said: Rather, he was called that for his torturing people with pegs.

Those who said this:

⁕ Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn told us, saying: Aḥmad ibn al-Mufaḍḍal told us, saying: Asbāṭ told us, from al-Suddī, regarding His saying ﴿the one of the pegs﴾, that he said: "He would torture people with pegs; he would torture them with four pegs, then raise a rock which was stretched with ropes, then it would be dropped upon him and crush him."

⁕ I was told by ʿAlī ibn al-Haytham, from Ibn Abī Jaʿfar, from his father, from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, who said: "He would torture people with pegs."

Others said: The meaning of that is: the one of the structures (buildings), and they said: the structures are the pegs.

Those who said this:

⁕ I was told by al-Muḥāribī, from Juwaybir, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, regarding ﴿the one of the pegs﴾, that he said: "The one of the structures."

The most likely of the sayings concerning this, to the truth, is the saying of the one who said: it refers to the pegs, either for torturing people or for play, for which they played for him; this is because that is the known meaning of "pegs." As for Thamud and the people of Lot, we have already mentioned the reports about all of these earlier in this book of ours. ﴿And the companions of the Thicket﴾ means: and the companions of the thicket (al-ghayḍah).

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ used to say, as I was told by Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā, from Abū ʿAmr: "al-Aykah: a dense cluster of acacia (nabiʿ) and lote trees (sidr), and it is the intertwined part of it." A poet said:

Afa-min bukāʾi ḥamāmatin fī aykatin ... yarfaḍḍu damʿuka fawqa ẓahri al-maḥmali

[The verse is by ʿAntarah al-ʿAbsī (Mukhtār al-Shiʿr al-Jāhilī, with the commentary of Muṣṭafā al-Saqqā, Ḥalabī edition, p. 387), and it is the fourth verse of a poem in which he satirizes Qays ibn Zuhayr, leader of Tamīm in some of its wars with ʿAbs. Its commentator said: al-Aykah is the dense, intertwined growth of trees. Tarafat dumūʿuka: they flowed. Al-maḥmal: the sword's strap. Abū ʿUbayda cited it in Majāz al-Qurʾān (folio 213-1), saying: "al-Aykah: al-ḥarajah: of nabiʿ and sidr, and it is the intertwined. A man said, while leaning on ʿAntarah: 'Afa-min bukāʾ...' the verse, meaning the sword's carrying-strap, which is the ḥamālah and al-ḥamāʾil. The plural of al-maḥmal is maḥāmil. Some of them say 'Laykah', without cutting the alif, and they did not know its meaning." End.]

That is, the sword's strap.

Ahl al-taʾwīl (the interpreters) said things similar to what we have said on this.

Those who said this:

⁕ Bishr told us, saying: Yazīd told us, saying: Saʿīd told us, from Qatādah, regarding ﴿and the companions of the Thicket﴾, that he said: "They were companions of trees, and most of their trees were the dawm (doum palm)."

⁕ Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn told us, saying: Aḥmad ibn al-Mufaḍḍal told us, saying: Asbāṭ told us, from al-Suddī, regarding His saying ﴿and the companions of the Thicket﴾, that he said: "The companions of the ghayḍah."

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they await but a single Cry; there will be no respite from it﴾ [38:15] ﴿And they say: "Our Lord, hasten to us our portion (qiṭṭ) before the Day of Reckoning"﴾ [38:16]

He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And they await but a single Cry﴾ — meaning these polytheists among Quraysh — ﴿a single Cry﴾, by which is meant the first blast in the Trumpet (ṣūr). ﴿There will be no respite from it﴾ — meaning: that Cry will have no interval (fawāq), that is, no slackening or cessation.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said things similar to what we have said.

Of those who said so:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying (And they await but a single Cry), meaning: the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿there will be no respite from it﴾.

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: al-Muharibi narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn Rafi', from Yazid ibn Ziyad, from a man of the Ansar, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah finished creating the heavens and the earth, He created the Trumpet (ṣūr) and gave it to Israfil, who places it at his mouth, fixing his gaze on the Throne, awaiting when he will be commanded." Abu Hurayrah said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the Trumpet?" He said: "A horn (qarn)." He asked: "What is it like?" He said: "A great horn into which three blasts will be blown: the blast of terror (fazaʿ), the first; the second is the blast of swooning (ṣaʿq); and the third is the blast of rising for the Lord of the worlds. Allah will command Israfil with the first blast, and he will say: 'Blow the blast of terror.' Then the people of the heavens and the people of the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills. Allah will command him and he will prolong it and extend it, and it will not slacken. This is the one of which Allah says: ﴿And they await but a single Cry; there will be no respite from it﴾."

The interpreters differed regarding the meaning of His saying ﴿there will be no respite from it﴾ (mā lahā min fawāq). Some of them said: it means that there will be no return or reversion for that Cry.

Of those who said so:

ʿAli narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿there will be no respite from it﴾ — he says: "no repetition (tardīd)."

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿there will be no respite from it﴾ — he says: "no return."

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿there will be no respite from it﴾: he said, "no return."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿there will be no respite from it﴾ — meaning the Hour; there will be no return or reversion from it.

Others said: rather, the meaning is that these polytheists will have after that no recovery (ifāqah) and no return to the world.

Of those who said so:

Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿there will be no respite from it﴾ — he says: "They will have no recovery after it, nor any return to the world."

Others said: the Cry in this place is punishment, and the meaning of the statement is: these polytheists await only a punishment that will destroy them, with no recovery from it for them.

It is one of the evidences of Abu ʿUbaydah (Majaz al-Qur'an, folio 213/1), who said regarding His saying "rabbanā ʿajjil lanā qiṭṭanā": al-qiṭṭ is the book. Meaning by the qiṭūṭ: the plural of qiṭṭ, which are the written records of rewards.

Some of them said: they only asked their Lord to hasten their share of the punishment prepared for them in the Hereafter, into this world, as some of them said: ﴿If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment﴾ [8:32].

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿And they say: "Our Lord, hasten to us our qiṭṭ before the Day of Reckoning"﴾: he said, "They asked Allah to hasten the punishment for them before the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from ʿAnbasah, from Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿for us qiṭṭanā﴾: he said, "our punishment."

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿hasten to us our qiṭṭanā﴾: he said, "our punishment."

Bishr narrated to me, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And they say: "Our Lord, hasten to us our qiṭṭanā before the Day of Reckoning"﴾: that is, our share, our portion of the punishment before the Day of Resurrection. Others said: their request was their share of Paradise, but they asked that it be hastened for them in this world.

Of those who said so:

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Thabit al-Haddad, who said: I heard Sa'id ibn Jubayr say regarding His saying ﴿hasten to us our qiṭṭ before the Day of Reckoning﴾: "Our share of Paradise."

Others said: rather, they asked their Lord to hasten sustenance (al-rizq).

Therefore we said that their request was for their portions of good and evil as I have mentioned.

He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And they await but a single Cry﴾ — meaning these polytheists among Quraysh — ﴿a single Cry﴾, by which is meant the first blast in the Trumpet (ṣūr). ﴿There will be no respite from it﴾ — meaning: that Cry will have no interval (fawāq), that is, no slackening or cessation.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said things similar to what we have said.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying (And they await but a single Cry), meaning: the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿there will be no respite from it﴾.

Abu Hurayrah said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the Trumpet?" He said: "A horn (qarn)." He asked: "What is it like?" He said: "A great horn into which three blasts will be blown: the blast of terror (fazaʿ), the first; the second is the blast of swooning (ṣaʿq); and the third is the blast of rising for the Lord of the worlds. Allah will command him and he will prolong it and extend it, and it will not slacken. This is the one of which Allah says: ﴿And they await but a single Cry; there will be no respite from it﴾."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 38, verses 17–20:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength. Indeed, he was constantly turning back (to Allah) (17). Indeed, We subjected the mountains to exalt [Allah] with him at dusk and at sunrise (18), and the birds gathered, all of them returning to Him (19). And We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom and decisive speech (20).﴾

Exalted is His remembrance, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): O Muhammad, be patient over what the polytheists of your people say to you, of the things you dislike in their speech to you, for We will test you with hardships just as We tested all Our messengers before you. Then We will make you, and those who oppose and defy you, subject to Our practice concerning the messengers whom We sent to Our servants before you. Among them was Our servant Ayyub and Dawud son of Iyshah, so remember him, the possessor of strength. By His saying ﴿dhal-ayd﴾ (the possessor of strength) He means: the possessor of power and severe might in the cause of Allah, and of patience in obeying Him.

⁕ Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding his saying ﴿Dawud dhal-ayd﴾, the possessor of strength in obedience to Allah.

* *

And His saying ﴿Indeed, he was constantly turning back (awwab)﴾

He means: Indeed Dawud was one who returns, turning from what Allah dislikes to what pleases Him. Awwab is derived from their saying: "Aba al-rajul ila ahlihi," meaning the man returned to his family.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said this:

⁕ Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to us, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿Indeed, he was awwab﴾, he said: one who returns from sins.

⁕ al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿Indeed, he was awwab﴾, he said: the one who returns from sins.

⁕ Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding his saying ﴿Indeed, he was awwab﴾, he said: the one who glorifies (Allah).

It is mentioned that when Dawud glorified [Allah], the mountains glorified with him.

Qatada used to say in this place:

⁕ Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿And the birds gathered﴾: subjected.

* *

And His saying ﴿all of them returning to Him﴾

* *

And His saying ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾

The interpreters differed regarding the meaning by which his kingdom was strengthened. Some said: it was strengthened by soldiers and men; he was guarded every day and night by four thousand, four thousand.

Mention of those who said this:

⁕ Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾, he said: he was guarded every day and night by four thousand, four thousand.

Others said: what strengthened his kingdom was that he was given awe from people because of a judgment he had passed.

Mention of those who said this:

⁕ Ibn Harb related to me, saying: Musa related to us, saying: Dawud related to us, from 'Alba' ibn Ahmar, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that a man from the Children of Israel sought redress against a man of their nobles, and the two gathered before Dawud the Prophet (ﷺ). The complainant said: This one seized my cows from me. Dawud asked the man about that, and he denied it. Then he asked the other for evidence, and he had no evidence. Dawud said to them both: Stand until I consider your matter. So they left his presence. Then Allah revealed to Dawud in a dream that he should kill the man against whom redress was sought. He said: This is a vision, and I will not hasten until I am certain. Then Allah revealed to Dawud again in a dream that he should kill the man, and Allah revealed to him a third time that he should kill him, or the punishment from Allah would come to him. So Dawud sent to the man: Allah has revealed to me that I should kill you. The man said: You would kill me without evidence and without verification?! Dawud said to him: Yes, by Allah, I will surely carry out the command of Allah concerning you. When the man realized that he was going to kill him, he said: Do not hasten against me until I inform you. By Allah, I was not seized for this sin, but I had secretly killed this one's father, and for that I am being killed. So Dawud ordered him to be killed. Then the awe of the Children of Israel for Dawud increased at that time, and his kingdom was strengthened by it. This is the saying of Allah: ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾.

The most correct of these statements, in our view, is to say: Allah, blessed and exalted, informed that He strengthened the kingdom of Dawud, and the text does not specify that this strengthening was by soldiers and armies alone, to the exclusion of the awe people had for him, nor the awe of people for him to the exclusion of the armies. It is possible that his strengthening was by some of what we have mentioned, and it is possible that it was by all of it. No statement is more correct regarding this than the word of Allah, since no report requiring submission has specified one of the meanings of strengthening.

Others said: rather, the meaning is: decisive speech, by requiring the claimant to produce evidence and the defendant to take an oath.

Mention of those who said this:

⁕ Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Dawud ibn Abi Hind informed us, saying: al-Sha'bi or another related to me, from Shurayh, that he said regarding His saying ﴿decisive speech﴾: the evidence of the claimant, or the oath of the defendant.

⁕ Yaqub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech﴾, he said: I was informed from Shurayh that he said: two witnesses or an oath.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Mansur, from Tawus, that Shurayh said to a man: This one finds fault with me over what was given to Dawud: the witnesses and the oaths.

⁕ Ibn al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far related to us, saying: Shu'bah related to us, from al-Hakam, from Shurayh, that he said regarding this verse ﴿decisive speech﴾: the witnesses and the oaths.

⁕ 'Imran ibn Musa related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Warith related to us, saying: Dawud related to us, from al-Sha'bi, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech﴾, he said: an oath or a witness.

⁕ Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿decisive speech﴾: the evidence upon the claimant and the oath upon the one claimed against; this is decisive speech.

Others said: rather, it is the saying "amma ba'd" (as for what follows).

Mention of those who said this:

⁕ Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Jabir ibn Nuh related to us, saying: Isma'il related to us, from al-Sha'bi, regarding His saying ﴿decisive speech﴾, he said: a man's saying: "amma ba'd".

The most correct of these statements, in our view, is to say: Allah informed that He gave Dawud, may Allah's blessings be upon him, decisive speech. Al-fasl is cutting off, and al-khitab is address. Whoever cuts off one man's address to another, when one of them is judging between them, the judge cuts off the matter between the judge and his opponent with a correct ruling; and whoever cuts off his address to his companion by obliging the addressed party to what is due upon him in judgment, if he is the claimant, by establishing evidence for his claim, and if he is the defendant, by imposing the oath if his opponent requests it. And whoever cuts off address, which is a sermon at the end of one story and the beginning of another, separates them with "amma ba'd." Since all of that is possible under the apparent meaning of the report, and there is no indication in this verse as to which of these is intended, nor has any established report from the Messenger (ﷺ) been transmitted about it, the correct position is that the report is general, as Allah made it general, so it is said: Dawud was given decisive speech in judgment, in discourse, and in sermons.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 38, verses 17–20:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength. Indeed, he was constantly turning back (to Allah) (17). Indeed, We subjected the mountains to exalt [Allah] with him at dusk and at sunrise (18), and the birds gathered, all of them returning to Him (19). And We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom and decisive speech (20).﴾

Exalted is His remembrance, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): O Muhammad, be patient over what the polytheists of your people say to you, of the things you dislike in their speech to you, for We will test you with hardships just as We tested all Our messengers before you. Then We will make you, and those who oppose and defy you, subject to Our practice concerning the messengers whom We sent to Our servants before you. Among them was Our servant Ayyub and Dawud son of Iyshah, so remember him, the possessor of strength. By His saying ﴿dhal-ayd﴾ (the possessor of strength) He means: the possessor of power and severe might in the cause of Allah, and of patience in obeying Him.

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said on this matter.

Dawud said to them both: Stand until I consider your matter. So they left his presence. Then Allah revealed to Dawud in a dream that he should kill the man against whom redress was sought. He said: This is a vision, and I will not hasten until I am certain. Then Allah revealed to Dawud again in a dream that he should kill the man, and Allah revealed to him a third time that he should kill him, or the punishment from Allah would come to him. And His saying ﴿and decisive speech (fasl al-khitab)﴾

The interpreters differed regarding its meaning. Some said: it means that he was taught judgment and understanding of it.

Mention of those who said this:

⁕ Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech﴾, he said: he was given understanding.

⁕ Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn Idris related to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿decisive speech﴾, he said: correctness in judgment and understanding of it.

⁕ Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿decisive speech﴾, he said: the knowledge of judgment.

⁕ Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him wisdom and decisive speech﴾, he said: the disputes in which people dispute before him, that decisive speech is the speech of understanding, and correctness in judgment and evidences.

Others said: rather, the meaning is: decisive speech, by requiring the claimant to produce evidence and the defendant to take an oath.

Mention of those who said this:

⁕ Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Dawud ibn Abi Hind informed us, saying: al-Sha'bi or another related to me, from Shurayh, that he said regarding His saying ﴿decisive speech﴾: the evidence of the claimant, or the oath of the defendant.

Whoever cuts off one man's address to another, when one of them is judging between them, the judge cuts off the matter between the judge and his opponent with a correct ruling; and whoever cuts off his address to his companion by obliging the addressed party to what is due upon him in judgment, if he is the claimant, by establishing evidence for his claim, and if he is the defendant, by imposing the oath if his opponent requests it. Others said: what strengthened his kingdom was that he was given awe from people because of a judgment he had passed.

Mention of those who said this:

⁕ Ibn Harb related to me, saying: Musa related to us, saying: Dawud related to us, from 'Alba' ibn Ahmar, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that a man from the Children of Israel sought redress against a man of their nobles, and the two gathered before Dawud the Prophet (ﷺ). The complainant said: This one seized my cows from me. Dawud asked the man about that, and he denied it. Then he asked the other for evidence, and he had no evidence. Dawud said to them both: Stand until I consider your matter. So they left his presence. Then Allah revealed to Dawud in a dream that he should kill the man against whom redress was sought. He said: This is a vision, and I will not hasten until I am certain. Then Allah revealed to Dawud again in a dream that he should kill the man, and Allah revealed to him a third time that he should kill him, or the punishment from Allah would come to him. So Dawud sent to the man: Allah has revealed to me that I should kill you. The man said: You would kill me without evidence and without verification?! Dawud said to him: Yes, by Allah, I will surely carry out the command of Allah concerning you. When the man realized that he was going to kill him, he said: Do not hasten against me until I inform you. By Allah, I was not seized for this sin, but I had secretly killed this one's father, and for that I am being killed. So Dawud ordered him to be killed. Then the awe of the Children of Israel for Dawud increased at that time, and his kingdom was strengthened by it. This is the saying of Allah: ﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾.

The most correct of these statements, in our view, is to say: Allah, blessed and exalted, informed that He strengthened the kingdom of Dawud, and the text does not specify that this strengthening was by soldiers and armies alone, to the exclusion of the awe people had for him, nor the awe of people for him to the exclusion of the armies. It is possible that his strengthening was by some of what we have mentioned, and it is possible that it was by all of it. No statement is more correct regarding this than the word of Allah, since no report requiring submission has specified one of the meanings of strengthening.
